opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm not at OpenAI anymore, so I don't have any inside information. I can only guess based on the general trend of the field, like everyone else.

If I had to bet, I think the main theme will still be agents. Over the past year we've watched models go from chatting to actually doing things: writing code, browsing the web, operating a computer, doing deep research. OpenAI has been pushing in that direction, and I'd expect them to release something that feels more like a real agent product. You give it a task that takes not five minutes but maybe hours, and it can plan, use tools, recover from mistakes, and come back with something usable.

Underneath that, I'd expect continued progress on reasoning models, the o-series line of thinking. RL on top of strong base models has turned out to be very powerful, and there's still a lot of headroom: longer reasoning, better tool use inside the reasoning, better efficiency so it's cheaper and faster. So maybe a new generation of models that unifies the reasoning model and the general chat model, so users don't have to pick which model to use.

Coding is probably where we'll see the most concrete jumps, because it's the domain where RL works best. You have clear feedback: the tests pass or they don't. I wouldn't be surprised if coding agents get good enough that people delegate whole features rather than individual functions.

What I'm less sure about is whether we'll see a single "wow" moment like ChatGPT in 2022. Progress now is more continuous. Each release is better, but the improvements show up most on hard, long-horizon tasks, which ordinary users may not notice right away. So my expectation is less a magical new thing and more agents that actually work reliably enough to be useful in daily work. If that happens, it's a big deal, even if it doesn't look as dramatic.

r001.rationale: The response predicts agent and model releases by the end of 2025, but does not say these are capabilities OpenAI already possesses or predict a wave of them being publicly released.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing everyone expects is that there will be a new flagship model, whatever they end up calling it. OpenAI has been pretty clear that they want to merge the GPT series and the o-series, so instead of users picking between a chat model and a reasoning model, there's one system that decides on its own how much to think. I'd be surprised if that unification doesn't ship in some form.

The second thing I'd bet on is agents. Not just a model that answers questions, but something that can actually operate a browser, use tools, finish a multi-step task for you. They've already put out early versions of that, and I think by the end of the year the push is going to be toward making it reliable enough that ordinary people use it, not just developers playing with it.

And then the third piece, which people talk about less, is the coding side. Everyone in this space is competing hard on code right now, and OpenAI is not going to leave that to Anthropic. So I'd expect stronger coding models and more of a product around them.

What I'm personally more curious about, from a research angle, is not the product list. It's whether we see real progress on reinforcement learning at scale beyond math and code. Those domains are easy because you can verify the answer. The hard question is whether they figure out how to apply the same recipe to messier tasks where there's no clean reward signal. If something ships that shows they've cracked that, even partially, that would be more significant to me than any single model release.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts a flagship model, agents, and coding advances by year-end, but does not clearly say OpenAI will publicly release a wave of capabilities it already possesses. It only notes that early agent versions have already been released.

astra-6.text: My guess is that we’ll see more capable reasoning models and agents that can handle longer, more complex tasks. The question is how reliably they can do that—whether they can carry a task through, recognize mistakes, and recover without someone constantly guiding them. I’d also expect tighter integration of voice, vision, and tool use. But I don’t have inside information about OpenAI’s roadmap, so I’d be cautious about predicting a particular release or date.

I’d also expect improvements in voice, video, and how models use tools. But I don’t have inside information about OpenAI’s release plans, so I’d treat those as predictions rather than promises. The thing I’d watch most closely is reliability: can a system complete a useful task consistently, rather than just give an impressive demonstration?
